content: The performance of early warning indicators (EWIs) for HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) is categorized as follows: good performance is defined as greater than 85%, passable performance is greater than 75%, and immediate remediation is required if the performance is 75% or less. In many settings, it is not feasible to collect key population-specific data through routine program monitoring, necessitating the use of surveys. Surveillance of HIV drug resistance in adults receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) focuses on acquired HIV drug resistance. Data collection should include sex, pregnancy or breastfeeding status at ART initiation, and age. For paper-based systems, age categories are typically divided into under 15 years and 15 years or older. If routine reporting is not available, annual data extraction should include more detailed age groups: under 5 years, 5–9 years, 10–14 years, 15–19 years, 20–24 years, 25–49 years, and 50 years or older. Retention in ART programs is measured at 12 months and provides insights into the reasons for non-retention, such as death, loss to follow-up, or treatment discontinuation. However, distinguishing between these outcomes can be challenging due to silent transfers and unreported deaths. Consequently, the interpretation of outcomes and the magnitude of loss to follow-up should be approached with caution and further investigation. ART adherence at the population level can be evaluated using on-time antiretroviral (ARV) drug pick-up as a proxy measure. While this method has limitations, it is practical and useful in resource-limited settings. For HIVDR EWIs, good performance is defined as greater than 90%, and passable performance is greater than 80%. The World Health Organization (WHO) HIV drug resistance early warning indicators assess program performance, including ART retention and viral load (VL) testing. By the 15-month mark, all patients on ART should have received at least one VL test. This indicator evaluates the availability of VL testing in a country. Data collection should include sex and age, with minimum age categories for paper-based systems being under 15 years and 15 years or older. For electronic systems, data can be disaggregated into 5-year age groups. Viral load suppression is the most reliable measure of patient adherence to ART. Specific levels of VL suppression can be expected in cohorts of patients who have initiated ART and continued treatment over time. These data can be compared to established benchmarks to assess program performance. The HIVDR EWI on ARV stock-outs monitors the percentage of months in a reporting year without ARV drug stock-outs, assessing the performance of the supply chain system. Continuous stock availability at all sites is essential for effective program delivery. ART survival rates are measured as the percentage of people living with HIV who are alive at 12, 24, and 36 months after ART initiation. These measures provide insights into true survival rates among ART patients and highlight potential misclassification, silent transfers, and unreported deaths. Tracking these outcomes can support program improvement by identifying ways to enhance patient tracking and data capture. Preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV is critical to reducing pediatric HIV-related mortality. Without treatment, half of all children with HIV will die before the age of two. Older children and adolescents may acquire HIV through sexual transmission or injecting drug use. Most infections in children under 15 years are due to MTCT, while new infections in those aged 15 and older are primarily due to unprotected sex or injecting drug use with contaminated equipment. Children and adolescents living with HIV represent a diverse group with varying prevention and treatment needs. The cascade of care for HIV-infected infants and children mirrors that of adults, encompassing diagnosis, linkage to care, enrollment, treatment, and viral suppression. However, collecting, organizing, reporting, and interpreting strategic information for children living with HIV presents unique challenges. Age disaggregation is essential for monitoring and evaluating the pediatric HIV care cascade. As children grow, their care and treatment needs evolve, necessitating age-specific approaches to service delivery. The standard age categories for disaggregating HIV-related data are: under 1 year, 1–4 years, 5–9 years, 10–14 years, and 15–19 years. Age disaggregation is particularly important for ART initiation, as all HIV-diagnosed children under five years are eligible for treatment. Starting ART in the first months of life significantly reduces mortality. Detailed age disaggregation can reveal gaps in ART coverage and inform planning for age-appropriate service delivery. Tracking children through the cascade of care is challenging due to the multiplicity of service points where HIV-infected children are identified and enrolled in care. These include referral hospitals, antenatal care (ANC) clinics, ART sites, maternal and child health (MCH) settings, immunization clinics, and well-child clinics. Children are often diagnosed at one facility and referred to another for care, with subsequent transfers to other sites for treatment. This fragmentation increases the risk of gaps in care due to insufficient linkages between services and loss to follow-up. Unique identifier codes and computerized information systems can improve data linkage over time and across services, enhancing patient tracking. Monitoring the pediatric HIV care cascade requires age-disaggregated data on indicators such as HIV testing, linkage to care, ART initiation, viral load suppression, and HIV drug resistance. Programs should assess HIV diagnosis strategies and uptake and retention in care to address low treatment and care coverage rates. Infants identified as HIV-positive should start ART immediately, while HIV-exposed infants require follow-up until their final HIV status is determined. Infected infants and children may drop out of the care cascade at various stages, leading to higher mortality rates. Quality-of-care indicators monitor the effectiveness of programs addressing children and adolescents, helping to identify gaps and improve early diagnosis and treatment strategies.
